The Crocodile icefish Chaenocephalus aceratus produces relatively large, yolk-laden eggs with a diameter of approximately 4.4 mm, and from this egg size the wet weight at birth has been estimated at 0.045 grams [Wwb = 0.045 grams]. Field surveys in the Southern Ocean indicate that newly emerged yolk-sac larvae, after an incubation period at seawater temperatures of -1 °C [T = -1 °C], typically hatch after around 60 days [ab = around 60 days]. This protracted embryonic development is characteristic of notothenioids and reflects the metabolic constraints imposed by the chronically cold polar waters they inhabit. The total length at metamorphosis, when the pelagic larva undergoes body plan reorganisation and transitions to a benthic juvenile, is approximately 8 centimeters . This morphological transformation marks a critical ecological shift, as the juvenile must begin foraging independently in the demersal zone. The species exhibits a slow, determinate growth pattern typical of high-latitude fishes, with asymptotic body size eventually constrained by the limited seasonal productivity of its environment. The maximum recorded adult body mass reaches 978 grams [Wwi = 978 grams], a value derived from length–weight regressions based on extensive trawl samples collected during austral summer research cruises.

Sexual maturation in Chaenocephalus aceratus occurs at markedly different sizes between the sexes, a pattern of sexual size dimorphism that is well documented among channichthyids. Females attain sexual maturity at a total length of 61.5 centimeters [Lp = 61.5 centimeters], while males reach puberty at a smaller size of 50.6 centimeters [Lp = 50.6 centimeters]. These size thresholds correspond to distinct body masses, with females weighing approximately 634 grams [Wwp = approximately 634 grams] at the onset of gonadal activity and males weighing approximately 371 grams [Wwp = approximately 371 grams] at the same developmental stage. The timing of puberty, measured as time since birth under the prevailing thermal regime of -1 °C [T = -1 °C], is estimated at approximately 2,373 days [tp = approximately 2,373 days], equivalent to roughly six and a half years. This delayed maturation is a common feature of Antarctic notothenioids and is thought to be an adaptive response to the extreme seasonal fluctuations in food availability, allowing individuals to accumulate sufficient energy reserves before investing in reproductive effort.

The reproductive output of Chaenocephalus aceratus is characterised by a high annual fecundity, typical of broadcast-spawning marine teleosts. Adult females produce a large number of eggs per spawning event, with the daily reproduction rate estimated at 62 eggs per day [Ri = 62 eggs per day] when measured under the species' natural environmental conditions of -1 °C [T = -1 °C]. This value, extrapolated from direct observations of gravid females during the spawning season, reflects the combined effect of a single annual reproductive event and the total egg complement per female. The extended lifespan of this species, with a maximum longevity of 20 years [am = 20 years] recorded under the cold stable conditions of -1 °C [T = -1 °C], permits multiple reproductive episodes over the course of an individual's life. This iteroparous strategy, coupled with the high fecundity, helps buffer the population against the high levels of natural mortality experienced during the extended egg and larval stages.

Comparative studies among channichthyid icefishes reveal that Chaenocephalus aceratus attains a relatively large ultimate total length of 72 centimeters [Li = 72 centimeters], placing it among the larger members of its family. This asymptotic size, derived from von Bertalanffy growth models fitted to length-at-age data, is accompanied by a correspondingly high ultimate wet weight of 978 grams [Wwi = 978 grams]. The species' growth trajectory reflects the energetic trade-offs imposed by life in near-freezing waters, where metabolic rates are profoundly depressed. The individual growth rate is slow, and the maximum recorded longevity of 20 years [am = 20 years] at -1 °C [T = -1 °C] is consistent with the general pattern observed in other large notothenioids. The combination of a long lifespan, delayed maturity, and a relatively large body size suggests a life-history strategy oriented toward the accumulation of somatic mass over many years before initiating the energetically costly process of gamete production.

In addition to its life-history traits, Chaenocephalus aceratus displays a suite of physiological adaptations to the extreme cold of its Antarctic habitat. The absence of haemoglobin and functional erythrocytes in its blood is the most notable feature, resulting in a characteristically transparent or pale appearance. This unusual trait, shared with other members of the family Channichthyidae, greatly reduces blood viscosity and lowers the energetic cost of circulation at sub-zero temperatures. Field metabolic rates measured in free-swimming individuals are exceptionally low, consistent with the depressed metabolic demands of a sedentary, ambush-predator lifestyle. The species feeds predominantly on krill and other pelagic crustaceans, using its large mouth and reduced dentition to capture prey in rapid lunges. Population density estimates from trawl surveys suggest that Chaenocephalus aceratus is locally abundant on the continental shelf of the Antarctic Peninsula and the South Shetland Islands, where it occupies a key trophic role as both predator and prey within the Southern Ocean food web.
